Learned local models support yaw-only feedback

Matched model-based observation improves tracking and sideslip estimates relative to a fixed 20 m/s nominal observer. Removing sideslip from CT fitting still causes almost no tracking penalty. This experiment does not establish a need for federation or isolate learning from speed scheduling.

All 1350 cases completed

270 cases per configuration; all satisfy the inherited steering/sideslip bounds. No steering limiter activation, synthesis failure or numerical failure. All evaluated true-origin controller–observer spectral radii are below one. These are local linear diagnostics, not nonlinear stability certificates.

Matched observers use straight-running models reconstructed from the learned physical coefficients. Controllers use unchanged saved gains.

What changes when the observer uses the learned model?

With the yaw-only CT controller held fixed, changing Nominal to Matched reduces mean tracking RMSE by 47.32% (0.03464 → 0.01825°/s), and sideslip-estimation RMSE by 93.80% (0.23750 → 0.01474°). Tracking improves for all 90 vehicle averages, although only 249 of 270 individual speed cases improve. Mean steering-rate RMS changes by −1.10%; the observer improvement does not require a higher mean steering-rate RMS in this comparison.

Changing both controller and observer from Nominal/Nominal to YawOnlyCT/Matched reduces mean tracking RMSE by 64.61%, an absolute 0.03332°/s. Steering-rate RMS rises by 26.22% (2.980 → 3.761°/s). Report this control-effort tradeoff with the tracking benefit. No method was tuned separately.

The strongest tracking improvement is at 13 m/s: Nominal/Nominal has 0.10601°/s mean error, YawOnlyCT/Matched 0.02385°/s. At 29 m/s the corresponding values are 0.02383 and 0.01430°/s. Thus the overall gain is consistent across vehicles but strongly speed-dependent, with a large contribution from the low-speed condition.

Yaw-only versus full-state identification

With matched observers, mean tracking RMSE is 0.018216°/s for FullStateCT and 0.018251°/s for YawOnlyCT: a difference of only 0.0000354°/s (0.194%). YawOnlyCT gives lower tracking error for 40 of 90 vehicle averages and 119 of 270 cases. This is a descriptive near-tie, not a formal equivalence test.

Sideslip estimation is more sensitive: mean RMSE increases from 0.010263° to 0.014735° (+43.57%, absolute +0.004472°). The case-level 95th percentile rises from 0.01812° to 0.03720°. The maximum is 0.03584° versus 0.05584°. The increase is not uniform: yaw-only fitting improves the sideslip estimate for 39 of 90 vehicle averages. The ten largest positive vehicle differences account for 62.09% of the net mean increase; the median vehicle difference is +0.001718°.

These results show that the resulting sideslip errors have limited tracking consequences for this maneuver and controller; they do not prove that sideslip information is generally unnecessary.

What the nominal comparison does not isolate

The nominal observer uses one fixed 20 m/s LTI model at 13, 21 and 29 m/s. The matched observer uses both recipient-specific learned parameters and the correct test speed. Its advantage therefore combines physical-parameter learning and known speed dependence. A speed-scheduled observer built from unchanged nominal physical parameters is the missing comparison before attributing the whole gain to identification. Hold the learned controller fixed when comparing these observers.

The very high mean normalized innovation squared with the fixed nominal observer (about 57) versus about 0.86 with matched observers is consistent with substantial nominal model mismatch under the chosen covariance allowance. It is not a calibrated statistical consistency test: Q was prescribed, not estimated, and the plant is nonlinear.

The local yaw-only CT baseline remains strong. This test provides no evidence that federation is needed, nor does it compare a newly learned federated observer. Previous training data were collected with full-state feedback. A future complete sensing workflow must acquire new trajectories with the common nominal observer/controller, then refit from measured yaw and applied steering.

Recommended next step

First add the small speed-scheduled nominal-observer comparison, holding the learned controller fixed. It distinguishes knowledge of speed dependence from learned recipient parameters without refitting. Then, if the acquisition controller/observer passes its operating checks, generate new yaw-only acquisition trajectories and refit. Do not add plant complexity or change covariance settings merely to obtain a larger method gap.

Audit and reconstruction limits

Verified all checkpoint integrity/provenance records, 1350 noise hashes, observer designs, true-origin spectral radii, and regenerated aggregate tables. Reconstructed the 15 prespecified preview cases without fitting or tuning. Maximum absolute difference across recorded metric values: 2.06e-13; maximum saved-preview numeric difference: 9.33e-15. These maxima span different physical units and are numerical reproducibility diagnostics only.

Exact hash matches: 0/15. The original strict replay command rejects these cross-platform differences, as intended. Numerical agreement is checked at rtol=1e-10 and atol=1e-10, while original results and hashes remain unchanged. Full-resolution original arrays for all 1350 cases are not available here; only the selected 15 are independently reconstructed.
